justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mildly bullish near-term bias anchored around current price levels with modest upward drift built in across horizons. For the one-day estimate, I leaned on the assumption that prices tend to exhibit mean-reverting behavior over very short windows absent a major catalyst, so the estimate stays close to whatever the prevailing level is with a slight upward tilt reflecting the general long-run equity risk premium. The one-week estimate edges slightly higher, incorporating a continuation of any near-term momentum while acknowledging that weekly moves tend to cluster around small positive returns on average. The one-month estimate reflects a somewhat larger drift assumption consistent with historical average monthly returns for broad equity indices, while also accounting for the possibility that any short-term trend persists into the medium term.

Confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily using historical realized volatility as a baseline. Daily equity index volatility tends to run in the range of 1–1.5% annualized to a daily figure, which translates to fairly tight one-day bands. As the horizon extends to a week and then a month, uncertainty compounds, which is why the one-month interval is substantially wider than the one-day interval. I also factored in the current macro environment, which has shown elevated sensitivity to interest rate signals, inflation data, and geopolitical developments, all of which tend to fatten the tails of the distribution relative to a purely calm historical baseline.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals are numerous. On the downside, a surprise Federal Reserve statement signaling more aggressive tightening, a significant geopolitical escalation, a credit event in a systemically important financial institution, or a worse-than-expected earnings season could all drive prices well below the lower bound of any of these intervals. On the upside, a dovish pivot signal, a major geopolitical resolution, or a strong batch of economic data suggesting a soft landing could produce sharp rallies that breach the upper confidence bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon where sentiment shifts have more time to accumulate.

It is also worth acknowledging model uncertainty as a fundamental limitation here. These intervals assume a relatively stationary volatility regime, but volatility itself can spike suddenly and dramatically, as seen during events like the 2020 COVID crash or the 2022 rate shock. In such regimes, even a 90% confidence interval constructed from recent historical data could understate true tail risk, meaning the actual probability of an extreme outcome may be higher than the stated intervals imply.
